```{r}
#| label: setup
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(here)
  library(data.table)
})
here::i_am("reports-src/summary.qmd")
source(here("R/utils/config.R"))
source(here("R/utils/tables.R"))
load_config()
invisible(list2env(
  readRDS(get_data_path("outputs", "summary_env")), environment()
))

# Formatting only: every number comes from summary_env.rds (08)
num.fn <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
loss.fn <- function(x) num.fn(-x$estimate)
loss_ci.fn <- function(x) {
  sprintf(
    "%s (95%% CI %s to %s)",
    num.fn(-x$estimate), num.fn(-x$upper), num.fn(-x$lower)
  )
}
est_ci.fn <- function(x) {
  sprintf(
    "%s (95%% CI %s to %s)",
    num.fn(x$estimate), num.fn(x$lower), num.fn(x$upper)
  )
}
pct.fn <- function(count, n) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * count / n)

TRAJ <- config$trajectories
age.lst <- trajectories$age
classes.dt <- age.lst$classes
main.dt <- classes.dt[which.max(n)]
compared <- class_pathology$age$compared
faster.dt <- classes.dt[group == compared]
other.dt <- classes.dt[!group %in% c(main.dt$group, compared)]
predicted.fn <- function(class_label, at) {
  age.lst$predicted[class == class_label & time == at, fit]
}
at.fn <- function(g) pathology$at_slopes[group == g]
at_size.fn <- function(g) pathology$at_sizes[group == g, N]
class_path.dt <- class_pathology$age$summary
amyloid_pct.fn <- function(g) {
  class_path.dt[group == g, pct.fn(n_amyloid_positive, n_pet)]
}

# Model comparison quantities used in the text
comparison.dt <- age.lst$comparison
model.fn <- function(d, r, g) {
  comparison.dt[
    degree == d & random == r & n_classes == g
  ]
}
selected.dt <- comparison.dt[selected == TRUE]
best_bic.dt <- comparison.dt[which.min(bic)]
lower_bic.dt <- comparison.dt[bic < selected.dt$bic]
participants.fn <- function(n) {
  sprintf("%d participant%s", n, ifelse(n == 1, "", "s"))
}
bic_none_1 <- model.fn("Quadratic", "None", 1)$bic
bic_slope_1 <- model.fn("Quadratic", "Intercept and slope", 1)$bic
linear_selected.dt <- model.fn(
  "Linear", selected.dt$random, selected.dt$n_classes
)
analysed_participants <- age.lst$participants
dropped_single <- data$extract_participants - analysed_participants
at_modelled_n <- sum(pathology$at_sizes[group %in% pathology$at_modelled, N])

# Years since the first test
years.lst <- trajectories$years_since_baseline
y_classes.dt <- years.lst$classes
y_main.dt <- y_classes.dt[which.max(n)]
y_compared <- class_pathology$years_since_baseline$compared
y_faster.dt <- y_classes.dt[group == y_compared]
y_other.dt <- y_classes.dt[!group %in% c(y_main.dt$group, y_compared)]
y_predicted.fn <- function(class_label, at) {
  years.lst$predicted[class == class_label & time == at, fit]
}
y_comparison.dt <- years.lst$comparison
y_model.fn <- function(d, r, g) {
  y_comparison.dt[degree == d & random == r & n_classes == g]
}
y_selected.dt <- y_comparison.dt[selected == TRUE]
y_slope_gain <- y_model.fn("Linear", "Intercept", 1)$bic -
  y_model.fn("Linear", "Intercept and slope", 1)$bic
y_quad_slope.dt <- y_comparison.dt[
  degree == "Quadratic" & random == "Intercept and slope" & n_classes >= 3
]
y_empty.dt <- y_comparison.dt[
  degree == "Linear" & random == "Intercept and slope" & min_class_n == 0
]
y_intercept_best.dt <- y_comparison.dt[random == "Intercept"][which.min(bic)]
y_class_path.dt <- class_pathology$years_since_baseline$summary
y_amyloid_pct.fn <- function(g) {
  y_class_path.dt[group == g, pct.fn(n_amyloid_positive, n_pet)]
}
y_tau_pct.fn <- function(g) {
  y_class_path.dt[group == g, pct.fn(n_tau_positive, n_tau)]
}
agreement.dt <- class_agreement
agree.fn <- function(a, y) {
  agreement.dt[class_age == a & class_years_since_baseline == y, sum(N)]
}
same_class_n <- agreement.dt[class_age == class_years_since_baseline, sum(N)]
```

# Purpose of this document

This document describes the analysis of longitudinal odour identification
in PREVENT-AD in enough detail to write it up and to defend it. For each
step it gives what was done, why, and which alternatives were considered and
rejected. Every number is computed by the analysis pipeline and inserted
automatically, so the text and the results cannot drift apart. The results
are preliminary and exploratory.

**Main findings.**

- Among `r analysed_participants` cognitively unimpaired participants,
  latent class models identified three trajectories of UPSIT score with age:
  a main class with slow decline that accelerates with age
  (`r num.fn(main.dt$pct, 0)`%), a faster-decline class
  (`r num.fn(faster.dt$pct, 0)`%), and a small class with very low scores
  throughout (`r num.fn(other.dt$pct, 0)`%). On years since the first
  test, adjusted for age at entry, the same three patterns appeared
  (`r num.fn(y_main.dt$pct, 0)`%, `r num.fn(y_faster.dt$pct, 0)`% and
  `r num.fn(y_other.dt$pct, 0)`%), and `r same_class_n` of
  `r analysed_participants` participants were in the same class on both.
- In the `r pathology$participants` participants with PET,
  amyloid-positive participants lost
  `r loss.fn(pathology$amyloid$positive)` UPSIT points per year, against
  `r loss.fn(pathology$amyloid$negative)` for amyloid-negative
  participants. Participants with both amyloid and tau (A+T+, n
  = `r at.fn("A+T+")$participants`) lost `r loss.fn(at.fn("A+T+"))` points
  per year. Scores at the first test did not differ by amyloid or tau status.
- Amyloid positivity was more frequent in the faster-decline class than in
  the main class, on age (`r amyloid_pct.fn(compared)` against
  `r amyloid_pct.fn(main.dt$group)`) and on years since the first test
  (`r y_amyloid_pct.fn(y_compared)` against
  `r y_amyloid_pct.fn(y_main.dt$group)`). This comparison is descriptive
  only.

# Data {#sec-data}

## Odour identification

The outcome is the total score of the University of Pennsylvania Smell
Identification Test (UPSIT), a 40-item forced-choice test scored from
`r data$score_range[1]` to `r data$score_range[2]` [@doty1984]. Only the
total score was used: item-level responses were not needed for the question,
and the total score is the clinically interpreted measure.

The extract contained `r data$extract_participants` participants and
`r data$extract_assessments` assessments. The following decisions defined
the analysis sample.

- **Date corrections.** In `r data$corrected_dates` follow-up assessments,
  the recorded date was the baseline date. The data provider supplied the
  correct dates, and the ages at those assessments were moved by the same
  interval.
- **INTREPAD 3-month retest excluded.** Visit `r data$excluded_visits`
  (`r data$excluded_visit_rows` assessments) exists only for participants in
  the INTREPAD trial, three months after baseline and during treatment.
  Keeping it would give trial participants an extra, very early assessment
  that observational participants do not have, which could create spurious
  differences in early trajectories between the two groups.
- **At least `r data$min_assessments` assessments.** A trajectory, and
  especially an individual rate of change, needs repeated measures.
  `r dropped_single` participants were excluded for this reason.
- **Participants with anosmia kept.** Excluding them would remove,
  by design, the low end of the outcome. The PI decided to keep them; they
  form most of the smallest class (Section [-@sec-classes]).

The analysis sample has `r analysed_participants` participants and
`r age.lst$assessments` assessments (median
`r age.lst$total$assessments_median` per participant), with a mean
follow-up of `r num.fn(age.lst$total$follow_up_mean, 1)` years (SD
`r num.fn(age.lst$total$follow_up_sd, 1)`) and a mean age at the first
test of `r num.fn(age.lst$total$age_mean, 1)` years (SD
`r num.fn(age.lst$total$age_sd, 1)`).

## Amyloid and tau PET

For each participant, the first PET scan was used. Amyloid is expressed in
Centiloids, a scale that standardises amyloid PET across tracers and
pipelines [@klunk2015]; amyloid positivity is a Centiloid value above
`r pathology$amyloid_cutoff`. Tau is the standardised uptake value ratio
(SUVR) in a temporal meta-region of interest; tau positivity is a value
above `r pathology$tau_cutoff`. Both cutoffs and positivity statuses come
from the data provider. Together they define amyloid/tau (A/T) groups in
the sense of the NIA-AA research framework [@jack2018].

Only the first scan was used because the question concerns pathology
status, and most participants have one scan. Of the
`r analysed_participants` participants in the analysis sample,
`r pathology$participants` have PET (`r pathology$amyloid_positive`
amyloid-positive), and `r pathology$with_tau` of them have a tau value
(`r pathology$tau_positive` tau-positive). One first scan has amyloid but no
tau, so that participant contributes to the amyloid analyses only.

The A/T groups are A−T− (n = `r at_size.fn("A-T-")`), A+T−
(n = `r at_size.fn("A+T-")`), A+T+ (n = `r at_size.fn("A+T+")`) and A−T+
(n = `r at_size.fn("A-T+")`). Tau positivity is rare, which shapes several
decisions below.

**Timing.** PET was acquired a median of
`r num.fn(pathology$years_to_pet_median, 1)` years after the first smell
test, and after the last smell test for
`r pathology$pet_after_last_upsit` participants. The pathology analyses
therefore relate smell change to pathology measured later in follow-up;
they cannot establish whether smell decline precedes pathology.

# Trajectory classes {#sec-classes}

## What the model does

The aim was to find out whether participants fall into groups with
different patterns of odour identification over time. Latent class
trajectory models do this. They assume the sample is a mixture of a small
number of unobserved classes, each with its own mean trajectory, and
estimate for each participant the probability of belonging to each class
[@naginodgers2010; @lennon2018].

Two variants exist. In group-based trajectory modelling (GBTM, also called
latent class growth analysis), everyone in a class follows the class
trajectory exactly, apart from independent measurement error
[@naginodgers2010]. In growth mixture modelling (GMM), participants also
vary around their class trajectory through random effects, as in an
ordinary mixed model [@muthen1999]. We fitted both and let the data decide
(Section [-@sec-selection]).

For participant $i$ at assessment $j$, in class $g$, the most general model
fitted is

$$
Y_{ij} = \beta_{0g} + \beta_{1g} t_{ij} + \beta_{2g} t_{ij}^2
  + u_{0i} + u_{1i} t_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij},
$$

where $Y_{ij}$ is the UPSIT score and $t_{ij}$ is age, centred at
`r TRAJ$age_centre` and divided by `r TRAJ$time_divisor` (so coefficients
are per decade from age `r TRAJ$age_centre`). The class-specific
coefficients $\beta_{\cdot g}$ define each class's mean trajectory. The
random intercept $u_{0i}$ and random slope $u_{1i}$ are each participant's
own deviation in level and rate. They follow a bivariate normal
distribution with unrestricted correlation, shared across classes, and
$\varepsilon_{ij}$ is normal measurement error. The quadratic term is
dropped in linear models; the random effects are dropped (GBTM) or reduced
to an intercept in simpler models. The probability of each class is
estimated together with the trajectories.

## Software: `lcmm` rather than `gbmt`

The models were fitted with the `hlme` function of the R package `lcmm`
[@proustlima2017], which fits both GBTM and GMM by maximum likelihood.
Its key property here is that it uses each participant's own assessment
times.

We first tried the R package `gbmt`. It requires every participant to be
measured at the same time points, because its likelihood compares the
predicted trajectory with observations on one shared grid. With age as the
time scale, every participant is tested at different ages, so `gbmt`
returned invalid fits (identical classes after a single iteration). `lcmm`
has no such restriction and also allows random effects, which `gbmt` does
not.

## Time scale: age

Age was chosen as the main time scale because odour identification
declines with age, and participants entered the study across a wide range
of ages. On age, a trajectory describes how smell changes over the lifespan
segment we observe, and participants who entered at different ages
contribute to different parts of the same curve.

The PI also asked for trajectories on years since the first test, with age
at the first test as a covariate. They are reported in Section
[-@sec-years] and agree closely with the classes on age.

## Models compared

We fitted a grid of `r age.lst$n_models` models: 1 to 5 classes, linear or
quadratic trajectories, and three random-effect structures (none, which is
the GBTM; a random intercept; a random intercept and slope).

Mixture models can converge to a local rather than the global maximum of
the likelihood, which gives a poorer solution that looks valid. To guard
against this, each model with more than one class was started from
`r age.lst$n_starts` random sets of initial values, generated around the
one-class estimates. Each start ran for `r TRAJ$gridsearch_maxiter`
iterations, and the best was then run to convergence (`lcmm::gridsearch`).
All `r age.lst$n_models` models converged. A first fit with fewer starts
reached the same selected solution; more starts changed some of the other
models, so the search is not infallible, and a solution reached by both
searches is more credible.

## Model selection {#sec-selection}

Models were judged on four criteria together, as recommended for latent
class trajectory models [@lennon2018; @vandeschoot2017]:

1. The Bayesian information criterion (BIC; lower is better), computed with
   the number of participants as the sample size.
2. Class sizes: a class of a handful of participants is not a reliable
   pattern.
3. Classification certainty: the mean posterior probability of the assigned
   class, per class. Values near 1 mean participants are clearly assigned.
4. Interpretability of the classes.

The full comparison is in @tbl-comparison (Appendix) and @fig-bic. The
reasoning was as follows.

- **Random effects are needed.** With one class, adding a random
  intercept and slope lowered the BIC from `r num.fn(bic_none_1, 0)`
  to `r num.fn(bic_slope_1, 0)`. Without random effects, ordinary differences
  between people in level and rate can only be represented by adding
  classes, so GBTM models tend to over-extract classes that are
  not distinct patterns. GMM separates these two sources of variation.
- **A lower BIC only through small, uncertain classes.** Of the
  `r age.lst$n_models` models, `r nrow(lower_bic.dt)` had a lower BIC than
  the selected one (`r num.fn(selected.dt$bic, 0)`). Each had more classes,
  a smallest class of `r min(lower_bic.dt$min_class_n)` to
  `r max(lower_bic.dt$min_class_n)` participants, and less certain
  classification: lowest mean posterior probability of a class
  `r num.fn(min(lower_bic.dt$min_appa, na.rm = TRUE))` to
  `r num.fn(max(lower_bic.dt$min_appa, na.rm = TRUE))`, against
  `r num.fn(selected.dt$min_appa)` for the selected model. The lowest BIC
  overall, of `r num.fn(best_bic.dt$bic, 0)`, belongs to a
  `r tolower(best_bic.dt$degree)` model with `r best_bic.dt$n_classes`
  classes whose smallest class has
  `r participants.fn(best_bic.dt$min_class_n)`.
- **Quadratic over linear.** With 3 classes and the same random effects,
  the quadratic model had a lower BIC than the linear one
  (`r num.fn(selected.dt$bic, 0)` against
  `r num.fn(linear_selected.dt$bic, 0)`), consistent with decline that
  speeds up with age.

The selected model therefore has `r age.lst$n_classes` classes,
`r tolower(age.lst$degree)` trajectories and a random intercept and slope.
Participants were assigned to their most likely class; the mean posterior
probability of the assigned class was
`r num.fn(age.lst$posterior_range[1])` to
`r num.fn(age.lst$posterior_range[2])` across classes, so classification
uncertainty is small.

## Results

```{r}
#| label: fig-trajectories
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-cap: !expr sprintf("**Three patterns of change in odour identification.** Class mean UPSIT by age with 95%% confidence bands, over individual participants coloured by their most likely class (%d participants, %d assessments).", age.lst$participants, age.lst$assessments)
knitr::include_graphics(age.lst$figure)
```

Between ages 60 and 80, the predicted mean of the main class
(`r main.dt$n` participants) fell from `r predicted.fn(main.dt$group, 60)`
to `r predicted.fn(main.dt$group, 80)` points, with most of the decline
after 70. The `r tolower(faster.dt$group)` class (`r faster.dt$n`
participants) started lower and fell from
`r predicted.fn(faster.dt$group, 60)` to
`r predicted.fn(faster.dt$group, 80)`. The `r tolower(other.dt$group)`
class (`r other.dt$n` participants) scored in the range of severe smell
loss throughout (`r predicted.fn(other.dt$group, 60)` points at 60); with
so few participants, the shape of its curve should not be interpreted.

The classes did not differ in age at the first test
(@tbl-classes). The `r tolower(faster.dt$group)` class had fewer women
(`r pct.fn(faster.dt$n_female, faster.dt$n)` against
`r pct.fn(main.dt$n_female, main.dt$n)`) and more APOE ε4 carriers
(`r pct.fn(faster.dt$n_apoe_carrier, faster.dt$n)` against
`r pct.fn(main.dt$n_apoe_carrier, main.dt$n)`). These differences are
descriptive; with `r faster.dt$n` participants, they are compatible with
chance.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-classes
#| tbl-cap: "**Characteristics of the trajectory classes.** At the first assessment; participants assigned to their most likely class."
create_class_table.fn(
  age.lst$class_table, title = NULL,
  source_note = "Differences between classes are descriptive."
) |>
  style_pdf_table.fn()
```

## How to describe the classes

Latent classes are a summary of heterogeneity, not proof that distinct
subpopulations exist. A defensible description is that the data are well
represented by three trajectory patterns, one of which shows faster
decline. Class membership is estimated with uncertainty, although here the
posterior probabilities are high. The smallest class mostly captures
participants with anosmia, whose scores are near the floor of the test.

## Years since the first test {#sec-years}

**Model.** Time is years since the first test (per decade in the model),
and age at the first test enters as a covariate, together with its
interaction with time, with effects shared by all classes. Without it,
participants who entered the study decades apart in age would partly be
sorted into classes by their age at entry, rather than by the shape of
their change. Otherwise the models and the grid are the same as on age.

**Search.** In a first fit with fewer starts per model, some models
reached a lower likelihood than simpler models nested in them. That
is impossible at the true maximum, so the search had missed the best
solution. The grid was re-fitted with `r years.lst$n_starts` starts per
model. More starts improved some fits but not all: the best start after
`r TRAJ$gridsearch_maxiter` iterations does not always lead to the best
solution. A solution the search reaches repeatedly is therefore more
credible than one found once. All `r years.lst$n_models` models converged.

**Selection.** The rule was the one used on age (@tbl-comparison-years,
@fig-bic-years).

- **Random slope.** With one class, a random slope on top of the random
  intercept lowered BIC by `r num.fn(y_slope_gain, 0)`: participants differ
  in their rate of decline. Models without it can express those
  differences only as extra classes; the best of them, with
  `r y_intercept_best.dt$n_classes` classes and a BIC of
  `r num.fn(y_intercept_best.dt$bic, 0)`, has classes of
  `r gsub("/", ", ", y_intercept_best.dt$class_pct)`%.
- **Linear rather than quadratic.** With a random intercept and slope,
  every quadratic model with 3 or more classes had a class of
  `r min(y_quad_slope.dt$min_class_n)` to
  `r max(y_quad_slope.dt$min_class_n)` participants, despite a lower BIC
  (`r num.fn(min(y_quad_slope.dt$bic), 0)` to
  `r num.fn(max(y_quad_slope.dt$bic), 0)`). Over the follow-up of this
  time scale, and with age at entry in the model, curvature is also less
  expected than over the age range.
- **Three classes.** The linear models with
  `r paste(y_empty.dt$n_classes, collapse = " and ")` classes reached the
  same solution as with `r y_selected.dt$n_classes` classes, with the
  extra classes empty. The 3-class solution was the same in the first fit
  and with `r years.lst$n_starts` starts.

The selected model has `r years.lst$n_classes` classes,
`r tolower(years.lst$degree)` trajectories and a random intercept and slope
(BIC `r num.fn(years.lst$bic, 0)`). The mean posterior probability of the
assigned class was `r num.fn(years.lst$posterior_range[1])` to
`r num.fn(years.lst$posterior_range[2])`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-trajectories-years
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-cap: !expr sprintf("**The same three patterns over years since the first test.** Class mean UPSIT with 95%% confidence bands for age %.1f at the first test (the sample mean), over individual participants coloured by their most likely class (%d participants, %d assessments).", years.lst$total$age_mean, years.lst$participants, years.lst$assessments)
knitr::include_graphics(years.lst$figure)
```

**Results.** Over 10 years from the first test, the main class
(`r y_main.dt$n` participants) went from
`r y_predicted.fn(y_main.dt$group, 0)` to
`r y_predicted.fn(y_main.dt$group, 10)` points, and the
`r tolower(y_faster.dt$group)` class (`r y_faster.dt$n` participants) from
`r y_predicted.fn(y_faster.dt$group, 0)` to
`r y_predicted.fn(y_faster.dt$group, 10)`. The
`r tolower(y_other.dt$group)` class (`r y_other.dt$n` participants) scored
in the range of severe smell loss throughout. The
`r tolower(y_faster.dt$group)` class was older at the first test than the
main class (`r num.fn(y_faster.dt$age_mean, 1)` against
`r num.fn(y_main.dt$age_mean, 1)` years; @tbl-classes-years): age at entry
is in the model, but its effect is shared by all classes, so class
membership can still differ by age.

**Agreement with the age classes.** Of the `r analysed_participants`
participants, `r same_class_n` were in the same class on both time scales
(@tbl-agreement). Of the `r faster.dt$n` participants in the
faster-decline class on age, `r agree.fn(compared, y_compared)` were also
in it on years. The faster-decline class on years is larger
(`r y_faster.dt$n` participants) because it also takes
`r agree.fn(main.dt$group, y_compared)` participants from the main class
on age. The two time scales therefore describe largely the same groups of
people.

```{r}
agreement_wide.dt <- dcast(
  agreement.dt[, .(
    class_age = factor(class_age, labels.v),
    class_years = factor(class_years_since_baseline, labels.v), N
  )],

)
gt::gt(agreement_wide.dt, rowname_col = "class_age") |>
  gt::tab_stubhead("Class on age") |>
```

# Pathology and rate of decline {#sec-pathology}

## Why not relate pathology to class membership

The obvious next step, testing whether pathology predicts class
membership, is not informative here. Only
`r class_path.dt[group == compared, n_pet]` participants of the
`r tolower(compared)` class have PET, so a test would have low power to
detect a difference of the size observed, and a non-significant result
would be uninterpretable. Classes also discard information: they reduce
each participant's trajectory to a label. We therefore asked the question
directly, with mixed models of the rate of change in all participants with
PET, and describe pathology by class without tests (Section
[-@sec-class-pathology]).

## Model

For each PET marker, a linear mixed model estimated each participant's
starting score and yearly change, and whether they differ by the marker:

$$
Y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 s_{ij} + \beta_2 M_i + \beta_3 M_i s_{ij}
  + \boldsymbol{\gamma}^\top \mathbf{X}_i
  + \boldsymbol{\delta}^\top \mathbf{X}_i s_{ij}
  + u_{0i} + u_{1i} s_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij},
$$

where $s_{ij}$ is years since the first test, $M_i$ is the marker,
$\mathbf{X}_i$ the covariates, and $u_{0i}, u_{1i}$ a random intercept and
slope per participant with unrestricted correlation. $\beta_3$ is the
difference in points per year associated with the marker, the quantity of
interest; $\beta_2$ is the difference at the first test. The models were
fitted by maximum likelihood with `lcmm::hlme` with a single class, which is
an ordinary linear mixed model; results were checked against `nlme::lme`
and were identical. Confidence intervals and p-values are Wald-based.

**Time scale.** Years since the first test, so that $\beta_1$ and
$\beta_3$ are directly in points per year. Age enters as a covariate.

**Covariates.** Age at the first test and sex, each with its interaction
with time, because both are related to smell and to amyloid and could
otherwise confound the association. Age at the first test was centred at
`r TRAJ$age_centre` and sex at the sample mean, so reference slopes are
for a participant aged `r TRAJ$age_centre` at the first test with the
sample's average sex balance. APOE ε4 and education were not in the main
models. APOE ε4 is a cause of amyloid accumulation, so adjusting for it
would remove part of the association of interest. Both were added in a
sensitivity analysis.

**Markers and separate models.** Four markers were modelled, each in its
own model: amyloid positivity, tau positivity, Centiloid (per
`r pathology$centiloid_step` Centiloids above
`r pathology$amyloid_cutoff`) and tau SUVR (per `r pathology$tau_step`
above `r pathology$tau_cutoff`). Amyloid and tau were not entered together
or with their interaction because tau positivity is rare and largely
overlaps amyloid positivity: the A−T+ and A+T+ cells have
`r at_size.fn("A-T+")` and `r at_size.fn("A+T+")` participants, too few to
separate the effects of tau and amyloid. Continuous markers use all the
information in the measure but assume a linear relation.

**A/T groups.** A separate model gave each of A−T−, A+T− and A+T+ its own
slope (`r at_modelled_n` participants). The A−T+ group
(n = `r at_size.fn("A-T+")`) was too small to estimate a slope and is not
shown, nor is the participant without tau.

**Missing PET.** Participants without PET are not in these models. The
models assume these PET data are missing at random given the covariates,
which cannot be checked with the data at hand.

## Results

```{r}
#| label: fig-pathology
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-cap: !expr sprintf("**Faster decline with amyloid and tau.** Predicted UPSIT over years since the first test, with 95%% confidence bands, for a participant aged %g at the first test with average sex (%d participants with PET).", TRAJ$age_centre, pathology$participants)
knitr::include_graphics(pathology$figure)
```

Amyloid-positive participants lost
`r loss_ci.fn(pathology$amyloid$positive)` points per year, against
`r loss_ci.fn(pathology$amyloid$negative)` for amyloid-negative
participants, a difference of `r loss_ci.fn(pathology$amyloid$difference)`
points per year. Tau-positive participants lost
`r loss_ci.fn(pathology$tau$positive)` points per year against
`r loss_ci.fn(pathology$tau$negative)`, a difference of
`r loss_ci.fn(pathology$tau$difference)`; with
`r pathology$tau_positive` tau-positive participants, this estimate is
imprecise. Each additional `r pathology$centiloid_step` Centiloids was
associated with `r loss_ci.fn(pathology$amyloid$per_step)` more points
lost per year, and each additional `r pathology$tau_step` SUVR with
`r loss_ci.fn(pathology$tau$per_step)`.

By A/T group, participants lost `r loss_ci.fn(at.fn("A-T-"))` points per
year with neither, `r loss_ci.fn(at.fn("A+T-"))` with amyloid alone and
`r loss_ci.fn(at.fn("A+T+"))` with both (@fig-pathology, @tbl-pathology).
The A+T+ estimate rests on `r at.fn("A+T+")$participants` participants.

Scores at the first test did not differ by amyloid (difference
`r est_ci.fn(pathology$amyloid$baseline)` points) or tau
(`r est_ci.fn(pathology$tau$baseline)`). The association is with the rate
of change, not with a single score. Adding APOE ε4 and education changed
the differences in slope little: `r loss.fn(pathology$amyloid$sensitivity)`
points per year for amyloid (`r loss.fn(pathology$amyloid$difference)` in
the main model) and `r loss.fn(pathology$tau$sensitivity)` for tau
(`r loss.fn(pathology$tau$difference)`).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pathology
#| tbl-cap: "**UPSIT change per year by amyloid and tau.** Linear mixed models adjusted for age at the first test and sex; also adjusted adds APOE ε4 carrier status and education."
create_pathology_table.fn(
  pathology$table,
  column_labels.lst = list(
    slope = "Change per year [95% CI]",
    difference = "Difference [95% CI]",
    p = "p",
    difference_sensitivity = "Also adjusted [95% CI]"
  ),
  title = NULL,
  source_note = "Negative values are points lost per year."
) |>
  style_pdf_table.fn()
```

# Pathology by trajectory class {#sec-class-pathology}

@tbl-class-pathology describes PET in each class. In the
`r tolower(compared)` class, `r amyloid_pct.fn(compared)` of participants
with PET were amyloid-positive, against `r amyloid_pct.fn(main.dt$group)`
in the main class. The difference is given with an approximate (Wald) 95%
confidence interval, which is wide. No p-values are reported: with so few
participants a test would have low power, and a non-significant result
could be misread as evidence of no difference. Tau positivity was rare in
every class.

On years since the first test (@tbl-class-pathology-years), the picture
was similar: `r y_amyloid_pct.fn(y_compared)` amyloid-positive in the
`r tolower(y_compared)` class against `r y_amyloid_pct.fn(y_main.dt$group)`
in the main class, and `r y_tau_pct.fn(y_compared)` tau-positive against
`r y_tau_pct.fn(y_main.dt$group)`, with
`r y_class_path.dt[group == y_compared, n_pet]` participants with PET in
that class.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-class-pathology
#| tbl-cap: "**Amyloid and tau PET by trajectory class.** First PET scan; descriptive only."
# Shorter row labels so the table fits the page width
class_path_table.dt <- copy(class_pathology$age$table)[
  , characteristic := gsub(
    ", difference from Main, percentage points", ", difference",
    sub(" (% of those with tau)", " (%)",
        sub(" (% of participants)", " (%)", characteristic, fixed = TRUE),
        fixed = TRUE)
  )
]
create_class_table.fn(
  class_path_table.dt, title = NULL,
  source_note = paste(
    "Differences from the main class are in percentage points with",
    "approximate (Wald) 95% confidence intervals. Tau percentages are of",
    "participants with tau."
  )
) |>
  style_pdf_table.fn()
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-class-pathology-years
#| tbl-cap: "**Amyloid and tau PET by trajectory class on years since the first test.** First PET scan; descriptive only."
y_class_path_table.dt <- copy(class_pathology$years_since_baseline$table)[
  , characteristic := class_path_table.dt$characteristic
]
create_class_table.fn(
  y_class_path_table.dt, title = NULL,
  source_note = paste(
    "Differences from the main class are in percentage points with",
    "approximate (Wald) 95% confidence intervals. Tau percentages are of",
    "participants with tau."
  )
) |>
  style_pdf_table.fn()
```

# Questions to expect

**Why a latent class model at all?** To describe heterogeneity in change
without imposing groups in advance. It shows that a minority declines
faster, which a single mixed model would average away.

**Why not the model with the lowest BIC?** BIC is one criterion among
several. On age, every model with a lower BIC than the selected one got
there by adding classes of `r min(lower_bic.dt$min_class_n)` to
`r max(lower_bic.dt$min_class_n)` participants, with less certain
classification; the lowest BIC belongs to a model whose smallest class has
`r participants.fn(best_bic.dt$min_class_n)`. Classes that small are not
reliable patterns.

**Why include random effects, when GBTM is the classic approach?** Without
them, between-person differences in level and rate are forced into extra
classes. Including them improved the fit markedly and gave fewer, clearer
classes.

**Could the search have missed a better solution?** For some models, yes:
on both time scales, going from a first fit with fewer starts to
`r age.lst$n_starts` starts per model changed some fits. The selected
models, however, were reached by both searches, so they are not artefacts
of one unlucky search. All models converged.

**Why two time scales, and do they disagree?** Age describes change over
the lifespan; years since the first test describes change within
follow-up, with age at entry as a covariate, which is closer to how a
clinical cohort is followed. Both found the same three patterns, and
`r same_class_n` of `r analysed_participants` participants were classified
the same way.

**Why is the years model linear when the age model is quadratic?** Model
selection followed the same rule on both. On years, the quadratic models
with 3 or more classes all had a class of 2 to 3 participants.

**Why are the pathology results not from the classes?** Too few
participants in the small classes have PET to test class differences
meaningfully. The mixed models use all participants with PET and the full
information in each trajectory.

**Why not adjust for APOE ε4?** APOE ε4 acts largely through amyloid, so it
is on the causal path. The sensitivity analysis shows the results hold when
it is added.

**Why separate amyloid and tau models?** Tau positivity is rare and mostly
occurs with amyloid, so a joint model cannot separate them. The A/T model
shows the combined picture.

**Does smell decline precede pathology?** These data cannot say. PET was
measured once, years after the first smell test.

**Were multiple comparisons corrected?** No. The markers are correlated
measures of the same process, the analyses are exploratory, and estimates
are reported with confidence intervals rather than as a set of tests.

# Limitations

- PET was measured once, a median of
  `r num.fn(pathology$years_to_pet_median, 1)` years after the first smell
  test; temporal order cannot be established.
- Tau positivity was rare (`r pathology$tau_positive` participants), so
  tau and A+T+ estimates are imprecise.
- The pathology models assume a linear decline over follow-up, whereas the
  age trajectories suggest decline accelerates with age. Age at the first
  test as a covariate partly accounts for this.
- Both model families assume normally distributed errors. UPSIT scores
  bunch near the top of the scale in healthy participants and near the
  bottom in anosmia, which these models handle only approximately. `lcmm`
  can fit models with non-linear links to the scale (`lcmm::lcmm`), a
  possible sensitivity analysis.
- Mixture-model searches can miss the best solution. The comparison tables
  show the best solution found for each model with
  `r age.lst$n_starts` starts, not a guaranteed optimum; the selected
  models were reached by two independent searches.

# Reporting

The GRoLTS checklist [@vandeschoot2017] lists what a paper using latent
trajectory models should report. This document covers the main items: the
software and estimation method, the time scale, the random-effect
structure, the number of random starts, the models compared, the selection
criteria and fit statistics of every model (@tbl-comparison), class sizes,
posterior probabilities, and plots of the estimated trajectories with the
observed data.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bic
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-cap: !expr sprintf("**Choosing the number of trajectory classes.** BIC of the %d fitted models by number of classes; the circle marks the selected model.", age.lst$n_models)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "**All fitted trajectory models on age.** BIC uses the number of participants. Posterior: lowest per-class mean posterior probability of the assigned class (missing when a class is empty)."
comparison_display.fn <- function(comparison.dt) comparison.dt[
  order(degree, random, n_classes),
  .(
    model = sprintf("%s, %s", degree, tolower(random)),
    n_classes,
    bic = num.fn(bic, 1),
    class_pct = gsub("/", " / ", class_pct),
    min_class_n,
    min_appa = ifelse(is.nan(min_appa), "–", num.fn(min_appa)),
    selected = ifelse(selected, "Selected", "")
  )
]
comparison_table.fn <- function(comparison.dt) {
  gt::gt(comparison_display.fn(comparison.dt), groupname_col = "model") |>
    gt::cols_label(
      n_classes = "Classes", bic = "BIC", class_pct = "Class sizes, %",
      min_class_n = "Smallest class, n", min_appa = "Posterior",
      selected = ""
    ) |>
    style_screen_table.fn() |>
    style_pdf_table.fn()
}
comparison_table.fn(comparison.dt)
```
